input: This worked example considers a continuous stirred-tank reactor, often referred to as a CSTR, which runs an esterification reaction that is first order in the limiting reactant. The purpose of the example is to determine the steady-state conversion that would be expected under ideal conditions in a reactor of this type. The rate constant for the reaction is 0.1 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time in the reactor is 50 min. On this basis, the steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 83.3%. This result is obtained under a particular set of assumptions that should be kept clearly in mind when the figure is interpreted. In particular, the estimate assumes perfect mixing throughout the vessel and constant density across the reactor. It is also important to note that tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. As a result, the conversion figure should be understood as the value associated with ideal CSTR behaviour under the stated assumptions, rather than as a measured or fully verified description of the performance of the real vessel. Overall, the example provides a clear benchmark value for the conversion, while also highlighting the respects in which the real system may depart from the idealised picture on which the calculation is based. The example is therefore valuable in two related respects. It shows how the kinetic information and the residence time combine under the ideal CSTR model to produce a definite conversion figure, and it also makes clear that the figure depends on idealisations that are built into the model from the outset. Where those idealisations are accepted, the result follows in a straightforward manner. Where the behaviour of the actual vessel is in question, the missing tracer information becomes the central limitation, because without it there is no direct evidence about how closely the vessel approaches the perfectly mixed condition assumed in the calculation.
target: A continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) runs an esterification that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.1 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 50 min. For an ideal CSTR at steady state, these values give a conversion of 83.3%. The conversion is a property of the ideal reactor model applied to the stated kinetics. Perfect mixing is assumed, so the composition and temperature are uniform through the vessel and the exit stream carries the vessel composition. Constant density is also assumed, so the residence time and the reaction rate are used on a single volumetric basis. The two assumptions define the reactor that the result describes. The actual vessel has not been characterised by tracer tests. Its residence-time behaviour is therefore unmeasured, and any departure from perfect mixing in the real vessel sits outside the estimate. The reported conversion is the ideal-CSTR value for the stated rate constant and residence time. It is a benchmark for the real vessel, not a measurement of it, and the absence of tracer data marks the point at which the benchmark stops short of describing the installed reactor. The example also shows what the ideal model does with the kinetic statement. First-order behaviour in the limiting reactant means that the rate follows the concentration of that reactant, and the CSTR balance then sets the steady state at which reaction within the vessel matches the flow of reactant through it. The conversion is the outcome of that balance under perfect mixing. Nothing in the result depends on a measured outlet composition; it is calculated from the rate constant, the residence time and the model. That is the strength of the figure as a teaching and design benchmark, and also its boundary. It states exactly what an ideal vessel would do with the stated kinetics, and it leaves the real vessel to be established by the tracer evidence that has not yet been obtained.
